title: Unit 18: Shaped by Wind as a Geomorphic Agent
sub: Reading: pages 260–273  ·  20 points  ·  15 minutes  ·  Closed book
instructions: Answer every question. For multiple choice, circle the single best answer. Write short answers in complete sentences.

questions.stem: Aeolian (wind) processes are most effective where surface material is
choices: rich in clay and bound by calcium carbonate
frozen for most of the year
fine, dry, and loose, with no vegetation cover
questions.why: p. 261 — vegetation imposes a frictional drag on the wind and binds soil particles down, so an environment without it is best. Clay-rich soils resist wind erosion because clay is cohesive.

questions.stem: What share of Earth’s deserts are partially or completely covered by sand?
questions.why: p. 261 — in most deserts wind erosion predominates over deposition, leaving a surface of stones rather than sand.

questions.stem: The cobblestone-like desert surface left behind after deflation removes the fine particles is called
questions.why: p. 262 — also called desert lag. The interlocking stones protect the surface beneath, which is why military activity in North African deserts during World War II caused lasting degradation.

questions.stem: Barchan (crescent) dunes have horns that point
questions.why: p. 267 — symmetrical barchans indicate wind from a constant direction. Parabolic dunes are the ones whose horns point upwind, anchored by vegetation or dampness.

questions.stem: Saltation accounts for approximately what share of sand transport over dunes?
questions.why: pp. 263–264 — traction, or surface creep, accounts for the 20–25%. Sand generally begins moving at a wind velocity of about 4.5 m/sec.

questions.stem: A flat area of clay, silt, or sand encrusted with salt, left behind when a shallow desert lake dries up, is called
questions.why: p. 271 — there are more than a hundred in North American deserts, most relics of Ice Age lakes. Lake Bonneville left the Great Salt Lake, Utah Lake, and Sevier Lake behind.

questions.stem: Parabolic dunes form where sand accumulates in a moist environment with a cover of vegetation.
questions.why: p. 268 — dampness and plants slow the dune’s base while the dry crest pushes ahead, leaving the horns anchored behind and producing the hairpin shape.

questions.stem: A mesa is defined as a flat-topped hill whose top is narrower than its height.
questions.why: That is a butte. Geographers use the rule of thumb that a mesa’s top is wider than its height; a butte is what remains when a mesa’s caprock has caved away to a small remnant. (pp. 271–273)

questions.stem: Explain the difference between deflation and abrasion, and name one landform produced by each.
questions.answer: Deflation is the lifting and removal of loose fine particles by the wind; abrasion is the sandblasting of rock surfaces by sand grains carried in the wind.
questions.rubric: 1 pt deflation defined, 1 pt abrasion defined, 1 pt for a valid landform for each. Deflation produces desert pavement (desert lag) and blowout depressions; the Qattara Depression in Egypt is partly a deflation feature. Abrasion shapes and polishes exposed bedrock, producing ventifacts (smooth faceted rocks) and, at larger scale, yardangs — elongate ridges streamlined parallel to the prevailing wind, which archaeologists think partly form the Great Sphinx of Giza. Credit noting abrasion is limited to a meter or two above the surface, since sand grains are not lifted far. (pp. 262–263)

questions.stem: Explain how mesas and buttes are formed through differential erosion.
questions.answer: Horizontally layered rocks are uplifted, then weathering and erosion strip the weaker layers away while a resistant caprock protects the rock beneath, leaving the resistant material standing above its surroundings.
questions.rubric: 1 pt — horizontally layered rocks are uplifted by tectonic activity, and rock types differ in their ability to resist weathering and erosion. 1 pt — weaker rocks such as shale erode into valleys while resistant types (sandstone, conglomerate, quartzite, basalt, chert, limestone, lava flows, and sills) remain topographically higher; a resistant sill or lava flow often forms the flat caprock. 1 pt — the sides break into a cliff-and-bench staircase, and basal sapping erodes the soft shale beneath until the cliff collapses and retreats. When only a small remnant of caprock is left, the mesa has become a butte. (pp. 272–273)
